say.text: A ventilated patient with acute cholecystitis needs a TG18 organ check. Which single blood gas result meets a Grade III respiratory criterion?

choices.label: PaO2 below 60 mmHg on room air
Arterial pH below 7.30 with a raised lactate
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: TG18 does not score the lungs on a raw oxygen level. It uses a ratio that takes into account how much oxygen the patient is being given.
Yes. TG18 scores the lungs on the PaO2/FiO2 ratio, and a value below 300 is a Grade III organ criterion.
The answer is the PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 300. TG18 grades the lungs by this ratio, and any one organ failure makes the grade III.
That is not the right choice.
A PaO2 of 60 is the everyday cut-off for respiratory failure in general medicine; TG18 scores the lungs on its own measure.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the everyday oxygen and acidosis numbers are the swap to avoid, because TG18 has its own organ thresholds.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A pH of 7.30 is an acidosis threshold from critical-care practice, and TG18 does not grade the lungs by pH.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the everyday oxygen and acidosis numbers are the swap to avoid, because TG18 has its own organ thresholds.

say.text: Before planning any procedure, a surgeon asks for the bile ducts to be imaged, with nothing passed into the duct yet. Which test fits?

choices.label: MRCP, an MR scan of the bile ducts
Diagnostic ERCP, with an endoscope and contrast
Contrast CT of the abdomen, portal venous phase
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which option passes no instrument into the duct at all.
Yes. MRCP is the non-invasive investigation of choice for bile duct stones, with no instrument passed.
The answer is MRCP. It is the non-invasive test for CBD stones, while ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic and is kept for when a stone is likely.
That is not the right choice.
ERCP is a good duct test, but it is invasive, and it is the treatment route once a stone is likely to need removing.
That is not the right choice.
CT is used for complications and other diagnoses, and it misses many gallstones in the duct.
A patient with acute cholecystitis is getting worse on treatment. You want to look for perforation, abscess or gas in the wall. Which test is used for complications?

choices.label: HIDA scan, a tracer uptake study of the gallbladder
Ultrasonography, a bedside study of the gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test shows the whole abdomen and its complications, not just whether the cystic duct is blocked.
Yes. CT is used for complications such as perforation, abscess and emphysematous cholecystitis, and to exclude other diagnoses.
The answer is CT. Ultrasound is the first test and HIDA is the most sensitive and specific for the diagnosis, but CT is used for complications.
That is not the right choice.
HIDA confirms cystic duct obstruction, but it is not the test used to look for complications such as perforation.
That is not the right choice.
Ultrasound is the initial test for gallstones, but looking for complications is the job of another test.
Which statement about timing of surgery for a fit patient with acute calculous cholecystitis is correct?

choices.label: Conservative care first, then interval surgery at 6 to 8 weeks
Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission
Antibiotics alone, with surgery only if symptoms recur
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The question asks for current practice, not the PYQ key. Ask what a fit patient gets during the index admission.
Yes. Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission, ideally within 72 hours, is current practice; the PYQ key expected interval surgery.
The answer is early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission, ideally within 72 hours of onset. The PYQ key expected conservative care then interval surgery.
That is not the right choice.
The 6 to 8 week plan is the older PYQ key, built on letting inflammation settle first, and it is not the current plan.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the older key and current practice differ here, and the key is what the PYQ expects.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Antibiotics alone leave the diseased gallbladder in place, and waiting for recurrence was the older key's habit.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the older key and current practice differ here, and the key is what the PYQ expects.

say.text: Which patient needs organ support and gallbladder drainage before any operation?

choices.label: A fit woman with Grade I disease and no organ failure
A fit man with Grade II disease in an experienced centre
A man with Grade III disease on noradrenaline
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Each grade has its own first step. Ask which patient has organ failure.
Yes. Grade III means organ dysfunction, so organ support and gallbladder drainage come first, and surgery follows later.
The answer is the Grade III patient. Grade I, and a fit Grade II, go to early laparoscopic surgery; Grade III is supported and drained first.
That is not the right choice.
She can go to early laparoscopic surgery, so she is not the one who needs support and drainage first.
That is not the right choice.
A fit Grade II patient can also go to early surgery, so drainage is not the first step for him.
Which statement about gallstones that cause no symptoms is correct?

choices.label: Most stay silent, and no routine treatment is needed
Ursodeoxycholic acid is first line to dissolve any silent stone
Every silent stone should be removed, as stones raise cancer risk

say.text: Yes. Most gallstones are silent, and symptoms develop at roughly 1 to 2 per cent a year, so expectant management is right.
The answer is that most silent stones need no treatment. Prophylactic surgery is kept for selected high-risk cases, such as a porcelain gallbladder.
That is not the right choice.
Dissolution works only for small radiolucent cholesterol stones in a working gallbladder, so the stone type comes first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: a silent stone is not treated by default, and tablets need specific stone qualifiers.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Stones carry a risk, but the yearly chance of symptoms is low, so routine surgery is not the default.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: a silent stone is not treated by default, and tablets need specific stone qualifiers.

say.text: Which of these is NOT part of Reynolds' pentad in acute cholangitis?
Yes. Charcot's triad is fever with rigors, jaundice and RUQ pain; hypotension and confusion make the pentad. Vomiting is in neither set.
The answer is vomiting. Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion makes Reynolds' pentad, and vomiting is in neither set.
That is not the right choice.
Hypotension is one of the two extra signs that make up the pentad, so it cannot be the odd one out.
That is not the right choice.
Confusion is the second extra sign in the pentad, so it cannot be the odd one out.
Bile is cultured from a patient with ordinary acute cholecystitis, and no gas is seen on any film. Which organism is most often grown?

choices.label: Klebsiella, as in any gas-forming infection
E. coli, the commonest organism in infected bile

say.text: Yes. E. coli is the commonest organism in infected bile; Clostridium perfringens is the one to think of when gas is present.
The answer is E. coli. With gas in the wall the cause is a gas-forming organism, most often Clostridium perfringens, but plain infected bile grows E. coli.
That is not the right choice.
Clostridium is the organism of emphysematous cholecystitis with gas, and this film shows none.
That is not the right choice.
Klebsiella is not the commonest in infected bile; E. coli holds that place.
Day two after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the drain shows green bile. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: Bile duct mistaken for cystic duct and divided
A blind clip across a bleeding vessel near the duct
Right hepatic artery injury in the triangle

say.text: Yes. Misidentifying the bile duct as the cystic duct is the commonest cause of major duct injury, which is why the view is confirmed before clipping.
The answer is misidentification of the bile duct as the cystic duct. That is the commonest cause of major duct injury, and the critical view prevents it.
That is not the right choice.
Bleeding is the dramatic complication, but it is not the commonest way the duct gets injured.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the most feared event is not the commonest cause of a duct injury.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
The hepatic artery sits near the duct, but injury to it is not the usual route to a major duct injury.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the most feared event is not the commonest cause of a duct injury.

say.text: A trainee says, 'I can see two tubular structures entering the gallbladder, so I will clip.' Which reply is right?

choices.label: Right, two structures is the whole critical view
Also clear the triangle and free the lower gallbladder
First dissect the cystic duct alone down to the bile duct

say.text: Yes. The critical view needs the triangle cleared, the lower gallbladder off the liver bed, and only two structures seen.
The answer: the triangle is cleared, the lower gallbladder is separated from the liver bed, and only two structures are seen. All three are required.
That is not the right choice.
Two structures is one of three requirements, not the whole view, so the other two must also be met.
That is not the right choice.
Chasing the cystic duct alone skips the triangle and the lower gallbladder, and the view depends on both.
A 70-year-old man is on day six in intensive care after cardiac surgery, on noradrenaline, with acalculous cholecystitis. What is the better first step?

choices.label: Open cholecystectomy today, to be safe

say.text: Yes. Unfit or critically ill patients with acalculous disease are drained first; a fit patient can be treated like calculous disease.
The answer is percutaneous cholecystostomy. Stasis and ischaemia in the critically ill make surgery risky, so the unfit patient is drained first.
That is not the right choice.
He is critically ill on a vasopressor, so an operation is not the first step; drainage is.
That is not the right choice.
A major operation in a patient this unstable is the risk to avoid, and the unfit patient is drained first.
A trainee writes, 'Gallstone ileus is the outlet block at the duodenum, and Bouveret's is the terminal ileum.' Which correction is right?

choices.label: No change; both statements are correct
Mirizzi is the outlet block, a stone in the bile duct lumen
Swap them; Bouveret's is the duodenum or pylorus

say.text: Yes. Bouveret's is gastric outlet obstruction from a stone in the duodenum or pylorus; gallstone ileus lodges in the terminal ileum.
The answer is to swap them. Bouveret's has the stone in the duodenum or pylorus; gallstone ileus obstructs the terminal ileum; Mirizzi compresses the hepatic duct from outside.
That is not the right choice.
The two sites are swapped here: gallstone ileus lodges in the terminal ileum, and Bouveret's is the outlet block.
That is not the right choice.
Mirizzi is a stone in Hartmann's pouch pressing on the hepatic duct from outside, not an outlet block.

cards.q: Which test is used to look for complications such as perforation, abscess or gas in the wall?
cards.a: Contrast CT. Ultrasound is the first test and HIDA is the most sensitive and specific for the diagnosis.

cards.q: Non-invasive investigation of choice for CBD stones?
cards.a: MRCP. ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic, so it is kept for when a stone is likely.
PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 300; any one organ dysfunction makes the grade III.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for acute calculous cholecystitis in a fit patient?
cards.a: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission, ideally within 72 hours.

cards.q: Asymptomatic gallstones: what is the default?
cards.a: Expectant management; symptoms develop at roughly 1 to 2 per cent a year.

cards.q: Where does gallstone ileus usually impact, and what is Rigler's triad?
cards.a: The terminal ileum. Rigler's triad: pneumobilia, small-bowel obstruction and an ectopic gallstone.

cards.q: Commonest cause of major bile duct injury?
cards.a: Misidentifying the common bile duct as the cystic duct; confirm the critical view before clipping.
